messages.subject: profiling develop branch
parts:
I profiled Rats in the developer branch, half the time
in warmup and half in sampling. I didn't profile any of
the I/O.

Nothing jumped out at me other than:

-- 4.2% of the time is evaluating check_range.

-- 5% of the processing time is spent on boost::math::detail::is_infinite

If the log probability isn't being called more, I'm not
sure what's going on, because the log prob and the gradient
calc are the bulk of the time.

- Bob

P.S. The Instruments profiler in Xcode works well, but the
template parameters make it very hard to read the functions (there's
a tool-tip-like popup, but it's one line and the function signature
doesn't fit).

You can attach it to a running process. Here's a basic guide:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/11445619/profiling-c-on-mac-os-x

(The pulldown is above the word "Target" --- I kept trying to
click on Target :-)).

Michael knows this code the best so will probably have the
easiest time understanding the output. All the template parameters
make it almost impossible to see what function's getting called.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] profiling develop branch
parts:
After profiling via Instruments and running various tests, the only cause I can offer at this point are copy constructors.

Firstly, the leapfrog code is pretty even, with the new code about 20% slower.  I believe a nontrivial amount of this is due to converting between Eigen::VectorXd and std::vector when calculating the gradient, the rest would be due to temporary allocations that arise in the refactoring (depending on how smart the template expressions are).

Secondly, Eigen copy constructors are f'ing slow.  At least 100 times slower than the std::vector copy constructor (estimate from my tests is about 200 times slower).  Because the new code uses Eigen for everything with lots of local copy constructions, it seems like this difference is adding up over the course of a long run and causing a big performance hit (the copy constructor of ps_point is almost 10% of the execution time).  I tried "#define EIGEN_NO_DEBUG" but it didn't have any effect on performance.

Thoughts?

On 5/29/13 8:56 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> After profiling via Instruments and running various tests, the only cause I can offer at this point are copy constructors.

> Firstly, the leapfrog code is pretty even, with the new code about 20% slower. I believe a nontrivial amount of this is
> due to converting between Eigen::VectorXd and std::vector when calculating the gradient, the rest would be due to
> temporary allocations that arise in the refactoring (depending on how smart the template expressions are).

This is where most of the time is, so that could account for
a large part of the issue.

> Secondly, Eigen copy constructors are f'ing slow. At least 100 times slower than the std::vector copy constructor
> (estimate from my tests is about 200 times slower).

WTF? I wonder if it's because they lean so heavily on
the curiously recursive template pattern that they
wind up having to iterate over the indices rather than
just copy memory? In this case, we could hack around the
issue by directly copying into their memory. That is,
rather than using the copy ctor, use a sized ctor, then
access it's memory and copy directly there. We know our
row and column order are right because we always use the
defaults.

When do you use copy constructors and can they be replaced
with references? I'm guessing Map is going to be even slower
than a copy constructor.

> Because the new code uses Eigen for everything with lots of local
> copy constructions, it seems like this difference is adding up over the course of a long run and causing a big
> performance hit (the copy constructor of ps_point is almost 10% of the execution time). I tried "#define
> EIGEN_NO_DEBUG" but it didn't have any effect on performance.

I'll take a closer look at ps_point and at the copy ctors in
Eigen and report back.

> Thoughts?

Nice profiling! I had a rather difficult time trying to read
through all the template parameters.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] profiling develop branch
parts:
I just ran some profiling and found some curious behavior.
The following two functions take the same amount of
time:

double fun1(const MatrixXd& x) {
MatrixXd y(x);
return y(0,0);
}
double fun2(const MatrixXd& x) {
MatrixXd y(x.rows(),x.cols());
std::memcpy(&y(0,0),&x(0,0),x.size() * sizeof(double));
return y(0,0);
}

Effectively all of the time's spent in either the copy constructor
or the memcpy (the matrix ctor in fun2 takes 0.1% of the time and
memcpy 99.9%.)

Then I tried vectors, and it's a very different story.
For vectors, fun1 takes 47% of the total time, fun2 25%,
and fun3 20%!

double fun1(const VectorXd& x) {
VectorXd y(x);
return y(2);
}
double fun2(const VectorXd& x) {
VectorXd y(x.size());
std::memcpy(&y(0),&x(0),x.size() * sizeof(double));
return y(2);
}
double fun3(const VectorXd& x) {
std::vector<double> y(&x(0),&x(0) + x.size());
return y[2];
}

Both fun2 and fun3 spend the same amount of time in memmve,
the rest of fun2's time being spent in the ctor.

WTF, indeed. So it looks like you can save about half
the amount of time spent in Eigen's copy ctors for vectors
by rolling your own with memcpy.

memcpy should be OK for everything we ever copy (double,
fvar, var).

I'm trying to test var now, but having trouble using var
as a header-only lib. I'll post a separate message about that.


- Bob
